newsitem.title: ITALY: New 'Green Revolution' needed to fight world hunger.
newsitem.headline: New 'Green Revolution' needed to fight world hunger.

text.p: Food workers are calling for a massive push by scientists to bring about a new "green revolution" needed to grow bigger crops and stave off hunger.
A quantum leap in crop yields on the scale of a similar technological revolution 30 years ago is vital to prevent millions more going hungry as populations explode, they say.

"We don't believe science has run out of ideas," Stein Bie, a senior official at the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation told reporters on Tuesday on the eve of the World Food Summit at FAO headquarters in Rome.
"We have to put resistance to the insects which eat farmers' crops into the genes of the plants themselves. And we have to make animals more resistant to disease," he said.
But delegates to the first summit called to fight famine are divided about how to resuscitate the agricultural revolution that saved Asia from mass hunger in the 1960s.

Varieties with nicknames like Super Soybean or Magic Maize invented with private patents in capitalist countries are fine for the rich man's plate, but do not help many poor-world farmers grow traditional subsistence crops, aid workers said.

U.S. officials preparing for the summit said many new techniques were being shared with developing countries but private firms also had a right to market their new inventions without seeing their ownership rights washed away.
New breakthroughs in food production are vital to ensure the five-day summit starting on Wednesday meets its target of halving world hunger within 20 years, FAO officials said.

The green revolution of the 1960s and 1970s depended on fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation to make room for high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice. Global cereal yields practically doubled between 1960 and 1990. Rice yields also soared, providing the springboard for Asia's breakneck economic growth in the 1990s, the U.N. agency said in a summit paper.

But with fertiliser use reaching saturation levels in some countries, scientists are now toying with genetic engineering to create crop varieties that environmentalists describe as a risky experiment with nature.
Greenpeace activists last week blockaded what they believed to be the first shipments to Europe of genetically altered soybeans developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto.

FAO officials warned reliance on seeds that have to be bought, rather than saved from crops grown at home, could exclude farmers in the one region which missed out on the last green revolution -- Africa, which also has the worst hunger.
A new green revolution needed to go beyond the research lab to make sure poor farmers shared the fruit of new research.
"We need to establish links between researcher and small farmers. If we don't, you will have magic rice, magic groundnuts produced in labs and never reaching the farmer," Bie said.
In many cases farmers were struggling to survive while research stations only a few miles way were growing food with yields three or even 10 times as high.
Aid workers called upon to educate farmers were left in offices without transport or basic necessities. Access to credit was also important to help poor farmers prosper.
FAO says using natural predators, such as spiders and wasps, to fight pests is one way of helping farmers boost crops without crippling costs or damage to the environment.
"Science has a lot up its sleeve but it will be at least 20 years before genetics and biotechnology come onstream for many small farmers," Bie said.
